title: Direct-to-Device: When Satellites Connect Your Phone

lines.speaker: Dr. James Park
lines.text: Mark, there's a narrative going around about d2d that I think misses the mark. People either think it's overhyped or they think it's going to change everything overnight. Where does the truth actually lie?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: (laughs) That's the perfect framing, because the truth is always in between. What's happening with when satellites connect your phone is real — it's not hype. But it's also not overnight. We've been working on this for years, and what people are seeing now is the result of a lot of unglamorous engineering and science that happened behind the scenes.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Welcome to TechNova. I'm Dr. Sarah Chen.

lines.speaker: Dr. James Park
lines.text: And I'm Dr. James Park. Today we're joined by Mark Matossian, Director of Space Systems at Google. Mark, welcome to the show.

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: Thanks for having me. Really glad to be here.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Mark, give us the honest state of d2d in Space as of mid-2026. Not the hype version — the real version.

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: The honest version is that we're at an inflection point. The breakthroughs in launch economics and reusability breakthroughs over the past eighteen months have been genuine — not just press releases, but real technical progress that you can measure. The key thing that's changed is satellite constellations has gone from theoretical to practical. We're no longer asking 'can this work?' — we're asking 'how do we scale it?'

lines.speaker: Dr. James Park
lines.text: What does that scaling look like in concrete terms?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: It means we're moving from bench-scale demonstrations to real-world deployment. The numbers I can share: we're seeing improvements in lunar and Mars exploration that are orders of magnitude better than where we were two years ago. And critically, the cost curve is bending in the right direction. When you combine better performance with lower cost, you get adoption, and that's what's happening now.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: What surprised you most in the last year?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: The speed. I expected progress, but the pace has been remarkable. commercial space stations advanced faster than I predicted, and regulatory framework turned out to be more tractable than we thought. When you have multiple breakthroughs happening simultaneously, they compound on each other, and that's when you get these nonlinear jumps.

lines.speaker: Dr. James Park
lines.text: Mark, let's talk about what's still hard. What are the problems that keep you up at night?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: The biggest one is space debris. It's the difference between something that works in the lab and something that works in production, every day, under real conditions. We've solved the science. What we haven't fully solved is the engineering — scientific missions, international competition, and the integration of all these components into a reliable system. That's the 80 percent of the work that nobody sees.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Can you give us a specific example of a problem you had to solve?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: Sure. Take investment landscape — six months ago, we were hitting a wall there. The conventional approach wasn't working, and we had to rethink the problem from scratch. What we ended up doing was satellite-centric — we restructured the entire approach around that, and it unlocked everything else. Sometimes the breakthrough isn't a new technique — it's a new framing of the problem.

lines.speaker: Dr. James Park
lines.text: How many people are working on these problems at your level?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: Globally? Maybe a few hundred people who truly understand the cutting edge. It's a small field, and the expertise is concentrated in a handful of teams. That's both a challenge and an opportunity — it means progress is bottlenecked by talent, but it also means that a single breakthrough from one team can advance the entire field.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: Mark, who else is working in this space, and how does your approach differ?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: There are several serious players. Some are taking the launch economics route, which is well-established but has limitations. Others are betting on reusability breakthroughs, which is newer and riskier but potentially more powerful. Our approach is different because we prioritize satellite constellations — most teams optimize for peak performance, but we optimize for reliability and cost at scale. That's what matters for real-world deployment.

lines.speaker: Dr. James Park
lines.text: Is this a winner-take-all market?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: I don't think so. The market is large and diverse enough that different approaches will win in different segments. The real competition isn't between the companies in this space — it's between d2d and the incumbent technology. We're all fighting to prove this is better than what exists today, and there's room for multiple winners once we do that.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: What about the investment environment? Is there enough capital flowing in?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: The capital is there — maybe too much, in some ways. The risk isn't lack of funding. It's that funding without focus leads to wasted effort. The companies that will succeed are the ones that can turn capital into concrete milestones — not more press releases, but real technical progress that moves the needle.

lines.speaker: Dr. James Park
lines.text: Mark, what should people be watching for in the next twelve to eighteen months?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: Three things. First, lunar and Mars exploration — we'll see meaningful progress there, and it'll be measurable. Second, commercial space stations — there are developments coming that the public doesn't know about yet, and they'll change the conversation. Third, the policy and regulatory side — regulatory framework is going to become a much bigger topic as the technology matures.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: If you could give one piece of advice to someone listening who's trying to understand where Space is heading, what would it be?

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: Don't trust the extremes — neither the hype that says everything changes tomorrow, nor the skepticism that says nothing will ever work. The truth is in the middle, and it's moving faster than most people realize. The best thing you can do is engage with the actual data — read the papers, look at the numbers, talk to the practitioners. The signal is there if you know where to look.

lines.speaker: Dr. James Park
lines.text: Mark Matossian, Director of Space Systems at Google. Thank you so much for joining us today.

lines.speaker: Mark Matossian
lines.text: Thank you both. This was a really enjoyable conversation.

lines.speaker: Dr. Sarah Chen
lines.text: And thanks to all of you for listening. This is TechNova — see you next time.
